senses.def: pertaining to an unshrunken condition of cloth, that is, before it has been washed and dried
the state of not being subject to death (that which will never die)
senses.comment: The clause ‘who alone is immortal’ may be expressed in some languages as simply ‘he is the only one who never dies’ or ‘he is the only one who always exists.’

senses.def: pertaining to what cannot be criticized
senses.comment: It may be necessary in some languages to restructure ἀκατάγνωστος and ἀνεπίλημπτος as complete clauses, so that instead of ‘sound words which are above criticism’ in Titus 2:8, one may translate ‘sound words which no one can criticize’ or ‘… against which no one can say anything.’ ‘Above reproach’ in 1 Timothy 6:14 may be rendered as ‘in such a way that no one can criticize it.’

senses.def: to leap or to jump into the air

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: the action of water forming bubbles and welling up from underneath the ground
senses.comment: In the NT ἅλλομαι[b] occurs only in the figurative context of John 4:14.|In some languages expressions referring to the flowing of water from a spring depend upon the extent or continuity of such a flow. If the spring is a perennial one, that is to say, if it flows all the time, it may be designated by one term, while if it is intermittent, that is, flows only during the rainy season, it may be referred to by quite a different term. There may also be distinctions as to whether the water flows out and then down or whether it actually comes up from below the surface. In John 4:14 the direction of flow is not important, but it is important to use a term which would indicate continuous flowing.

senses.def: the father of Josiah
the father of Ματταθίας[a]
to cause something to become new and different, with the implication of becoming superior
a marker of negatively linked elements
senses.comment: The phrase ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν in Matthew 10:29 is elliptical, for it presumes some type of involvement by God in such an event. Some have interpreted the phrase ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν as meaning ‘without your Father’s consent,’ while others interpret it as meaning ‘without your Father’s knowledge.’ The particular manner or mode of involvement by God must depend upon the broader context and not upon the meaning of ἄνευ.|The phrase ἄνευ λόγου in 1 Peter 3:1 is semantically equivalent to an event, for it means essentially ‘without their saying a word’ or ‘without them saying anything.’

senses.def: a city in Judea
to expect, with the implication of some benefit
to speak on behalf of oneself or of others against accusations presumed to be false
(derivative of ἀπολογέομαι ‘to defend oneself,’ 33.435) the content of what is said in defense
pertaining to not working

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to habitually refusing to work (probably with a more unfavorable connotation than in the case of ἄτακτος, 88.247)

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: pertaining to not giving careful consideration to something
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀργός in Matthew 12:36, see ἀργός[e] 72.21. It is also possible that ἀργός in Matthew 12:36 means useless (see ἀργός[d] 65.36).

senses.def: pertaining to being useless, in the sense of accomplishing nothing
pertaining to showing indifference as to whether something is as it should be
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἀργός in Matthew 12:36 as meaning ‘without thought’ (ἀργός[c] 30.44), ‘worthless,’ or even ‘useless’ (ἀργός[d] 65.36).

senses.def: chief tax collector, in the sense of one who controlled activities of certain other tax collectors
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ἀρχιτελώνης as meaning a principal or important tax collector rather than one who controlled the activities of other tax collectors.

senses.def: a marker of negatively linked elements
senses.comment: The phrase ἄτερ ὄχλου may be interpreted to mean ‘without the people knowing about it’ or ‘in the absence of the multitude.’

senses.def: pertaining to not being able to speak or talk
pertaining to being without meaning
senses.comment: Rather than use a double negative expression in rendering this phrase in 1 Corinthians 14:10, it may be better in many languages to use a positive expression, for example, ‘yet all can be understood’ or ‘yet all have meaning.’

senses.def: (derivative of βδελύσσομαι ‘to abhor,’ 25.186) that which is utterly detestable and abhorrent

(a fixed phrase derived from Hebrew, literally: the detestable thing of desolation) an abomination (either an object or an event) which defiles a holy place and thus causes it to be abandoned and left desolate
senses.comment: In translating βδέλυγμα, it may be necessary in some languages to use a phrase such as ‘that which God detests’ or ‘that which God hates’ or even ‘that which causes God’s anger.’ The term ἐρημώσεως may then be translated as ‘that which causes people to abandon’ or ‘that which causes something to be deserted.’ The entire phrase may then be translated in some languages as ‘that which God detests and which causes something to be abandoned’ or ‘… left desolate.’

senses.def: to assist in supplying what may be needed
to enter into a marriage relation, applicable either to a man or to a woman
a letter of the Greek alphabet
any kind of written document, whether in book or manuscript form, with focus upon the content

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: an object containing writing addressed to one or more persons, normally written on papyrus
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to try to distinguish between a letter as an object and a letter as content or message. In Acts 23:33 the focus seems to be upon the letter as an object, not necessarily upon the contents of the document. In most contexts, however, it is impossible to distinguish between a letter as a material object and a letter as a message (see 33.48).

senses.def: a written statement of financial accounts, especially of debts
senses.comment: In place of the expression ‘here is your account,’ one may say ‘here is a list of what you owe.’

senses.def: (pl; των n) the body of information acquired in school or from the study of writings
senses.comment: For a discussion of problems involved in translating John 7:15, see μανθάνω[a] (27.12).

senses.def: to cause someone to pay a tenth
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are problems involved in speaking of ‘a tenth,’ and accordingly there are difficulties in formulating expressions about ‘tithing.’ In some languages one may speak of ‘a tenth’ as ‘one part of ten parts’ or ‘one part together with nine parts.’ ‘To tithe’ may be rendered as ‘from ten parts to pay one part’ or ‘to pay one part and to keep nine parts.’

senses.def: to give a tenth of one’s income
senses.comment: In Hebrews 7:9 it may be important to indicate clearly that it was not Levi himself who received the tenth but his descendants. Therefore, one may render the latter part of Hebrews 7:9 as ‘Levi, whose descendants collect the tenth, also paid it.’

senses.def: to render assistance or help by performing certain duties, often of a humble or menial nature
senses.comment: In some languages it is essential in communicating the concept of ‘service’ to introduce a specific reference to ‘a servant,’ for example, ‘to help as a servant’ or ‘to assist as one who must,’ and in some contexts it may be useful to employ a phrase such as ‘to help in small things’ or ‘to do the low tasks.’|In rendering Matthew 20:28 it may be necessary to be somewhat more specific about those who serve or are served, for example, ‘the Son of Man did not come in order for people to serve him but in order to serve people.’

senses.def: to take care of, by rendering humble service to
senses.comment: In Matthew 25:44, it may be possible to render ‘and we did not take care of you’ as ‘and we did not give you whatever you needed.’

senses.def: to serve food and drink to those who are eating
to serve God in some special way, such as a deacon
senses.comment: It seems quite evident that διακονέω[d] involved a number of different functions as persons served others, especially in connection with relief to the poor. In some instances it may be best to translate διακονέω[d] as ‘to have responsibility to help others’ or ‘to be responsible to take care of the needs of believers.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to serve tables) to be responsible for financial aspects of an enterprise
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret the phrase διακονέω τραπέζαις not as an idiom but simply as ‘to wait on tables, to serve meals’ (see 23.26 and 46.13), but even so the context relates to caring for needs.

senses.def: to rot or decay, in reference to organic matter
the state resulting from not having drunk anything for a period of time
(figurative extension of meaning of διψάω[a] ‘to thirst,’ 23.39) to have a strong desire to attain some goal, with the implication of an existing lack
senses.comment: In Matthew 5:6 the two terms διψάω and πεινάω mutually reinforce the meaning of great desire.

senses.def: to give an object or benefit to someone, with the probable implication of greater formality than in the case of δίδωμι[a] (57.71)
an object which resembles a person, animal, god, etc. and which is an object of worship
senses.comment: The technical distinction between an image and an idol is that an image may merely represent a supernatural being, while an idol not only represents such a being but is believed to possess certain inherent supernatural powers. Images often become idols when they are assumed to possess such powers in and of themselves rather than being mere representations of some supernatural entity. If, for example, various images of a particular supernatural being are supposed to have different healing powers, then what began merely as images or representations of a supernatural power have become idols, in that the different images themselves have acquired special efficacy.|Though the existence of idols and corresponding terms for them are widespread, idols are by no means universal, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to employ some type of descriptive equivalent, for example, ‘objects that are made to look like gods’ or ‘carved statues that are considered to be gods.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of εἴδωλον[a] ‘idol,’ 6.97) an unreal supernatural being
senses.comment: A ‘false god’ may be rendered as ‘that which seems to be a god.’ In 1 John 5:21 one may speak of ‘those that seem to be gods but really are not.’|It is also possible, however, to interpret εἴδωλον in 1 John 5:21 as being simply an idol.

senses.def: to wonder greatly or to be very much amazed
to move out of or away from a place, with a possible implication of a considerable distance separating a person from the earlier location
to remain in the same place over a period of time
to continue in an activity or state
senses.comment: In Hebrews 8:9 the implication of ‘to continue in a covenant’ is to adhere to the articles or stipulations of a covenant. Accordingly, one may render Hebrews 8:9 as ‘because they did not remain faithful to my covenant.’ In Acts 14:22 (παρακαλοῦντες ἐμμένειν τῇ πίστει ‘encourage them to remain true to the faith’), it is also possible to translate the expression ‘to remain true to the faith’ as ‘to continue to believe.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to feel resentful because of what someone has done
to maintain a state of antagonism or hostility
senses.comment: In a number of languages hostility is expressed largely in psychological terms, for example, ‘to be angry at’ or ‘to have one’s heart curdle against,’ but hostility may also be expressed in terms of overt behavior, for example, ‘to turn against,’ ‘to face away from,’ or ‘to turn one’s back on.’

senses.def: to be under the control of or to be subject to someone or something
glosses: to be under the control of
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult or impossible to maintain the figure of ‘yoke’ in Galatians 5:1. An equivalent expression may be ‘do not become slaves again’ or ‘do not let people make you slaves again.’ Such a bold metaphor, however, must sometimes be changed to a simile: ‘do not, as it were, let yourselves be made slaves.’

senses.def: to give off or to reflect a very bright light
a part of the Roman Empire (usually acquired by conquest) and constituting an administrative unit ruled over by an ἔπαρχος selected by the Roman Senate
to take hold of or grasp, with focus upon the goal of the motion
senses.comment: In a number of languages quite different terms must be employed if one is to take someone by the hand in order to lead him or take someone by the hand in order to rescue him. The difference implied in the presumed force or strength required frequently results in quite different words being used.

senses.def: to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
(figurative extension of meaning of ἐπιλαμβάνομαι[a] ‘to grasp,’ 18.2) to learn something about someone, with the purpose of seizing, arresting, or overcoming
glosses: to learn in order to seize

senses.def: to assist in supplying what may be needed
senses.comment: Though the meaning of ‘help’ is possible for ἐπιλαμβάνομαι in Hebrews 2:16, the more generally accepted interpretation is ‘to be concerned with’ or ‘to take an interest in’ (see 30.42).

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to be concerned about, with the implication of possible help
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπιλαμβάνομαι in Hebrews 2:16, see 35.1.

senses.def: to experience some event or state, often with the implication of something negatively valued
senses.comment: In the expression in 1 Timothy 6:12, ἐπιλαβοῦ no doubt also suggests some activity associated with the state of eternal life.

senses.def: the full authority to carry out an assignment or commission
senses.comment: In Acts 26:12 the combination of ἐξουσία and ἐπιτροπή serves to reinforce the sense of complete authority.

senses.def: pertaining to being a different or strange language

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: pertaining to that which is particularly acceptable, and hence quite pleasing
senses.comment: In some languages the statement ‘an offering very acceptable to God’ (Romans 15:16) must be rendered as ‘an offering with which God is very pleased’ or ‘an offering which pleases God very much.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which is particularly favorable or propitious
suffering the loss of something which one has previously possessed, with the implication that the loss involves considerable hardship or suffering
one of the twelve apostles; see also 93.227
to come in contact with
senses.comment: It is also possible in Hebrews 11:28 that θιγγάνω is to be understood in the sense of ‘to kill’ (see 20.75).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of θιγγάνω[a] ‘to touch,’ 24.74) to cause the death of someone, perhaps suggesting some supernatural or mysterious means
a city in Judea, not far from the north end of the Dead Sea
pertaining to having power
pertaining to being physically strong and vigorous
a high point on a scale of extent and with the implication of strength involved in the activity or state

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to high status, probably on the basis of significant personal capacity
the son of Arphaxad in the genealogy of Jesus
the son of Enos in the genealogy of Jesus
(an idiom, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

senses.def: to step down forcibly upon, often with the implication of destruction or ruin

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of καταπατέω[a] ‘to trample on,’ 19.52) to thoroughly despise someone or something
(derivative of κατηγορέω ‘to accuse,’ 33.427) one who brings accusation
any large sea creature
a dye obtained from egg-clusters of a cochineal, collected from the leaves of Quercus coccifera
senses.comment: In Matthew 27:28 ‘scarlet robe’ may have implied high military rank.

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
steep slope, steep side of a hill
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs
to practice magic, presumably by invoking supernatural powers
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to share with someone else what one has
to recall information from memory, but without necessarily the implication that persons have actually forgotten
senses.comment: In some languages the process of remembering is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to find one’s thoughts again’ or ‘to see again in one’s heart’ or ‘to have one’s liver repeat the words.’

senses.subdomain: Recalling and Responding with Appropriate Action
senses.def: to recall or be aware of information, and as a result to respond in an appropriate manner (for example, punishing, helping, honoring, etc., depending upon the context)
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 11:2 the occurrence of μιμνῄσκομαι would seem to imply more than merely a mental state of recalling the presence of Paul in Corinth. The implication may very well be to mentioning Paul in prayer.

senses.def: (causative derivative of μωρία ‘foolishness,’ 32.57) to cause the content of certain thoughts to become devoid of meaning
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 1:20 the focus is upon the content of wisdom and nonsense, and it may be necessary to make this explicit, for example, ‘the people of the world thought that what they understood was wise, but God showed that their thoughts were foolish’ or ‘… their way of thinking was foolish.’

senses.def: (derivative of μωρός[a] ‘unwise, foolish,’ 32.55) to become one who does not employ a capacity to understand and thus acts very foolishly
to become insipid or tasteless
senses.comment: In Matthew 5:13 μωραίνομαι is equivalent to ἄναλος (5.27), that is to say, to be without a salt taste. Pure salt cannot actually lose its taste, but the sodium chloride of impure salt can be leached out, especially in humid weather, and the remaining substance is accordingly tasteless. See also discussion at 5.25.

senses.def: to win a victory over

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: one of a set of hard, bony structures set in the mouth of humans and many animals; used for chewing and biting
senses.comment: There are several problems involved in the rendering of ὀδούς. Even in the case of Revelation 9:8 it may be necessary to use two different terms for teeth, since human teeth may be referred to by expressions quite different from those used in referring to the teeth of animals. In Acts 7:54 the idiom ‘to grind one’s teeth’ denotes anger (88.184), but a literal rendering of ‘to grind the teeth’ may mean in some languages merely ‘to be nervous.’ The expression βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων ‘gnashing of the teeth’ is used in connection with the tortures of hell (Luke 13:28), but a literal rendering of such a phrase can be quite misleading, since it may refer merely to the eating of some hard substance. See 23.41.

senses.def: a cloud-like mass of moisture close to the earth's surface
senses.comment: In the NT ὁμίχλη is used only figuratively: οὗτοί εἰσιν πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι καὶ ὁμίχλαι ὑπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι ‘these men are dried up springs or mists blown along by a storm’ 2 Peter 2:17. The metaphorical usage in 2 Peter 2:17 must be marked in a number of languages as a simile, for example, ‘these men are like springs that have dried up and are like mists which the storm blows along.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὁρίζω ‘to set limits on,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to a definite decision or firm resolve

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role

long legless reptile; no eyelids or external ears; moves by wriggling or gliding; some species have a poisonous bite; symbol of lurking, unexpected danger; associated with lies, deception, and misleading teaching
senses.comment: Though ὄφις[a] may refer to any kind of snake, in Luke 10:19 it is obviously a reference to a poisonous snake that would harm a person who stepped on it. In translating Luke 10:19 it is essential to avoid an expression which will mean merely ‘to walk on snakes’ as though one were to walk for some distance over a mass of swarming snakes. The implication of this context is simply that one is able to step on snakes without being harmed.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ὄφις[a] snake, 4.52) a dangerous and despised person
senses.comment: One must exercise due caution in rendering ἔχιδνα in Matthew 12:34 and ὄφις in Matthew 23:33, since in some cultures snakes are regarded as being particularly wise and clever, and therefore an expression such as ‘brood of vipers’ could be a compliment. In some languages important distinctions are made between different types of snakes, and therefore connotations may vary considerably.

senses.def: to cause someone to suffer public disgrace or shame
senses.comment: The expression ‘to disgrace in public’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to cause everyone to think bad about’ or ‘to cause everyone to speak in whispers about.’

senses.def: to join surreptitiously with evil intent
glosses: to slip into a group unnoticed

senses.def: to be in a state of hunger, without any implications of particular contributing circumstances
senses.comment: Hunger is often spoken of in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘my stomach is crying,’ ‘my throat has been cut’ (implying that one has not been able to swallow food for a long time), or ‘my stomach is a deep hole.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of πεινάω ‘to hunger,’ 23.29) to have a strong desire to attain some goal, with the implication of an existing lack
senses.comment: In Matthew 5:6 the two terms διψάω and πεινάω mutually reinforce the meaning of great desire.

senses.def: to acquire possession of something, with the probable component of considerable effort

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to do something with regard to one’s life) to save or preserve one’s own life
(derivative of πλανάω[b] ‘to wander about,’ 15.24) one who or that which wanders about or around
senses.comment: In Jude 1:13 there appears to be a double-entendre in that πλανήτης may also suggest the meaning of πλανάω ‘to deceive, to cause to be mistaken’ (see 31.8). Therefore, such persons may be described not only as ‘wanderers,’ but as ‘deceivers.’ For a further discussion of πλανήτης in Jude 1:13, see 1.30.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the place or location in which one has the right to be a citizen
to be fitting or right, with the implication of possible moral judgment involved

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to think about something ahead of time, with the implication that one can then respond appropriately
glosses: to have in mind to do

senses.def: to move toward a reference point, with a possible implication in certain contexts of a reciprocal relationship between the person approaching and the one who is approached
a state of having insufficient possessions
to throw with considerable force
to put or place something down, with the possible implication of rapidity of action
to wave or possibly to throw something into the air
senses.comment: This symbolic action of throwing garments into the air or waving them violently was a means of indicating strong protest by an angry mob.|In a number of languages, however, such an expression would be interpreted as a sign of joyous agreement. One cannot change the nature of the event, but it may be essential to have some type of explanatory note to indicate the meaning of such an action.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ῥίπτω[a] ‘to throw,’ 15.217) to be or to become dejected, with a possible implication of loss of hope
(derivative of σάρξ[c] ‘people,’ 9.11) pertaining to physical human beings
senses.comment: In Hebrews 7:16 the phrase ‘human regulations’ can be rendered as ‘regulations made by people.’ For another interpretation of σάρκινος in Hebrews 7:16, see 26.8.

senses.def: pertaining to what is human or characteristic of human nature
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σάρκινος in Hebrews 7:16, see 9.13.

senses.def: pertaining to the natural, physical characteristics of persons and often including their characteristic behavior
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σάρκινος in 1 Corinthians 3:1, see 41.42.

senses.def: (derivative of σάρξ[f] ‘human nature,’ 26.7) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, but with special focus upon more base physical desires
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σάρκινος in 1 Corinthians 3:1, see 79.4.

senses.def: to refrain from speaking or talking
to lose or not have the ability to speak
glosses: to not be able to speak
senses.comment: It is possible that σιωπάω in Luke 1:20 means only ‘to say nothing’ or ‘to remain silent’ (33.117), in which case it would probably be better to reverse somewhat the order and translate ‘and you will not be able to speak but will remain silent until the day these things happen.’

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σιωπάω[a] ‘to be silent,’ 33.117) the process of becoming calm after a storm
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to translate σιωπάω[c] literally as ‘be still’ since this might imply continue to remain still. Since there is a change in state, it may be necessary to say become still or cease to be stormy.

senses.def: a soldier who acts as a courier to carry confidential information
senses.comment: In Mark 6:27 σπεκουλάτωρ may also have the meaning of ‘executioner’ (see 20.70).

senses.def: one who carries out official executions on the basis of orders from military or government officials
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret σπεκουλάτωρ (a borrowing from Latin) as meaning ‘courier,’ possibly a soldier who had special duties to carry messages of a confidential nature (see 33.196).

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the upper part of the digestive tract, especially the stomach
senses.comment: In 1 Timothy 5:23 it may be useful in some languages to translate ‘a little wine for the sake of your digestion’ or ‘… in order to help your digestion.’

senses.def: to converse with someone, including a clear implication as to reciprocal response
to happen, with the implication of that which one meets up with
a Christian woman in the church of Philippi
pertaining to being in a wretched state, either mentally or physically

senses.subdomain: Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
senses.def: four times as much in quantity

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.def: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering
senses.comment: The action of grinding one’s teeth in the case of an epileptic fit is so widespread that it is normally not difficult to find some way of expressing this type of action.

senses.def: to sing a song associated with religion and worship
glosses: to sing a song of praise

senses.def: a trough placed beneath the wine press to receive the grape juice pressed out
to cause someone not to be troubled
glosses: to prevent trouble happening to someone

senses.def: to keep oneself from doing something
a seaport on the south coast of Crete

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: agate, chalcedony, usually milky or gray in color (see 2.29)
(derivative of χρηματίζω[a] ‘to make known a divine revelation,’ 28.39) the content of a divine revelation or utterance
a particular melodic pattern with verbal content
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to use a combination such as ‘to sing a new song.’ One can, however, often use an expression such as ‘to sing with new words’ or ‘to utter a new song.’|In employing terms for ‘to sing’ or ‘song,’ it is important to avoid an expression which will apply only to some restricted type of music, for example, translated hymns using melodies from Western Europe.
